cards.evidence: Tidal volume (TV) is the amount of air that normally enters the lungs during quiet breathing, which is about 500 milliliters.

bw: Air left after a maximal exhalation
cards.tp: Residual volume makes breathing easier.

ww.Expiratory reserve volume (ERV): ERV is the extra air that can be exhaled past a normal tidal expiration.
ww.Tidal volume (TV): TV is the air moved in quiet breathing.

cards.evidence: Residual volume (RV) is the air left in the lungs if you exhale as much air as possible.

bw: Extra air forcefully exhaled past a tidal expiration
cards.tp: IRV is the extra volume brought in by a deep inhalation past a tidal inspiration.

ww.Inspiratory reserve volume (IRV): IRV is the extra air inhaled, not exhaled.

cards.evidence: Expiratory reserve volume (ERV) is the amount of air you can forcefully exhale past a normal tidal expiration, up to 1200 milliliters for men.

cards.tp: Vital capacity is between 4000 and 5000 mL.

ww.Total lung capacity (TLC): TLC includes the residual volume as well.

cards.evidence: Vital capacity (VC) is the amount of air a person can move into or out of his or her lungs, and is the sum of all of the volumes except residual volume (TV, ERV, and IRV), which is between 4000 and 5000 milliliters.

bw: Air remaining after a normal tidal expiration
cards.tp: Inspiratory capacity is TV plus IRV.

ww.Inspiratory capacity (IC): IC is the sum of tidal volume and inspiratory reserve volume.

cards.evidence: On the other hand, the functional residual capacity (FRC) is the amount of air that remains in the lung after a normal tidal expiration; it is the sum of expiratory reserve volume and residual volume (see Figure 22.18).

bw: About 6000 mL in men and 4200 mL in women
cards.tp: TLC is the total air held after a forceful inhalation (TV, ERV, IRV and RV).

ww.Vital capacity (VC): VC leaves out the residual volume.
ww.Inspiratory capacity (IC): IC is only TV plus IRV.

cards.evidence: For example, total lung capacity (TLC) is the sum of all of the lung volumes (TV, ERV, IRV, and RV), which represents the total amount of air a person can hold in the lungs after a forceful inhalation.

bw: Air in the airway that never reaches the alveoli
Takes no part in gas exchange
cards.tp: Alveolar dead space is air in alveoli that cannot function, for example from disease or abnormal blood flow.

ww.Alveolar dead space: This is air within alveoli that are not working, not air in the airway.
ww.Residual volume: RV is air left in the lungs after maximal exhalation and includes alveolar air.

cards.evidence: In addition to the air that creates respiratory volumes, the respiratory system also contains anatomical dead space, which is air that is present in the airway that never reaches the alveoli and therefore never participates in gas exchange.

bw: Normal respiratory rate of an adult
cards.tp: A child under 1 year has a normal rate of 30–60, and a 10-year-old about 18–30.

ww.30–60 breaths per minute: This is the normal range for an infant under 1 year.
ww.5–8 breaths per minute: This is far below the adult normal range.

cards.evidence: By adolescence, the normal respiratory rate is similar to that of adults, 12 to 18 breaths per minute.

bw: Medullary group that sets a steady rhythm
cards.tp: When DRG activity stops, the muscles relax and expiration occurs.

ww.Ventral respiratory group (VRG): The VRG is involved in forced breathing.
ww.Pneumotaxic center: The pneumotaxic center is in the pons and inhibits the DRG.

cards.evidence: The DRG is involved in maintaining a constant breathing rhythm by stimulating the diaphragm and intercostal muscles to contract, resulting in inspiration.

bw: Medullary group active in forced breathing
cards.tp: The VRG drives both forced inspiration and forced expiration.

ww.Dorsal respiratory group (DRG): The DRG maintains the constant quiet breathing rhythm.
ww.Apneustic center: The apneustic center is in the pons and controls depth of inspiration.

cards.evidence: The VRG is involved in forced breathing, as the neurons in the VRG stimulate the accessory muscles involved in forced breathing to contract, resulting in forced inspiration.

cards.tp: The pontine respiratory group has the apneustic and pneumotaxic centers.

ww.Pneumotaxic center: The pneumotaxic center inhibits the DRG and controls the overall rate.
ww.Ventral respiratory group (VRG): The VRG is in the medulla and drives forced breathing.

cards.evidence: The apneustic center is a double cluster of neuronal cell bodies that stimulate neurons in the DRG, controlling the depth of inspiration, particularly for deep breathing.

bw: Pontine center that inhibits the DRG
cards.tp: Together the apneustic and pneumotaxic centers form the pontine respiratory group.

ww.Apneustic center: The apneustic center stimulates the DRG and controls depth of inspiration.
ww.Dorsal respiratory group (DRG): The DRG is in the medulla and is inhibited by the pneumotaxic center.

cards.evidence: The pneumotaxic center is a network of neurons that inhibits the activity of neurons in the DRG, allowing relaxation after inspiration, and thus controlling the overall rate.

cards.tp: Rising CO2 increases brain H+, which triggers central chemoreceptors to deepen and speed breathing.

ww.Blood oxygen level: The source says the major stimulus is not oxygen concentration.
ww.Blood glucose level: Blood glucose is not a respiratory stimulus in the source.

cards.evidence: The major factor that stimulates the medulla oblongata and pons to produce respiration is surprisingly not oxygen concentration, but rather the concentration of carbon dioxide in the blood.

bw: Brain respiratory centers do not respond to rising CO2
cards.tp: Diaphragm and intercostals are not stimulated regularly, so breathing stops for a short period.

ww.Obstructive sleep apnea: This is caused by airway obstruction, with respiratory drive intact.
ww.Hyperpnea: Hyperpnea is forced breathing, not a pause in breathing.

cards.evidence: In central sleep apnea, the respiratory centers of the brain do not respond properly to rising carbon dioxide levels and therefore do not stimulate the contraction of the diaphragm and intercostal muscles regularly.

bw: Relaxed tongue and throat muscles, obesity
cards.tp: Excess neck adipose tissue can push soft tissue into the airway lumen.

ww.Central sleep apnea: Central apnea is a failure of respiratory drive, not a blocked airway.

cards.evidence: Obstructive sleep apnea is caused by an obstruction of the airway during sleep, which can occur at different points in the airway, depending on the underlying cause of the obstruction.

bw: Mask forcing air into the airway at regular intervals
cards.tp: Weight loss, avoiding alcohol and sleep position changes also help. Central apnea may need supplemental oxygen.

ww.Spirometer: A spirometer measures lung volumes and does not treat apnea.
ww.Nebulizer: A nebulizer delivers aerosolized drugs and is not described as apnea treatment.

cards.evidence: Treatment of sleep apnea commonly includes the use of a device called a continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) machine during sleep.

bw: Neck muscles that lift the thorax
cards.tp: Lifting the thoracic wall increases lung volume.

ww.Internal intercostals: Internal intercostals help compress the rib cage during forced expiration.

cards.evidence: During forced inspiration, muscles of the neck, including the scalenes, contract and lift the thoracic wall, increasing lung volume.

bw: Peripheral chemoreceptors drive breathing when O2 falls to
cards.tp: Chemoreceptors sense only dissolved oxygen, not oxygen bound to hemoglobin, so a large drop is required.

ww.100 mm Hg: This is a normal arterial oxygen level and does not trigger the response.
ww.80 mm Hg: The source gives about 60 mm Hg or less as the trigger.

cards.evidence: If blood oxygen levels become quite low—about 60 mm Hg or less—then peripheral chemoreceptors stimulate an increase in respiratory activity.

bw: Partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air
cards.tp: In the atmosphere the partial pressure of oxygen is about 159 mm Hg, and in oxygenated pulmonary vein blood about 100 mm Hg.

ww.About 40 mm Hg: This is the oxygen partial pressure of blood in the pulmonary capillaries and of tissues.
ww.About 160 mm Hg: This is close to the atmospheric value, not the alveolar value.

cards.evidence: The partial pressure of oxygen in alveolar air is about 104 mm Hg, whereas the partial pressure of oxygenated blood in pulmonary veins is about 100 mm Hg.

bw: Greater alveolar partial pressure of CO2
cards.tp: This lets CO2 be exhaled at a greater rate. Low blood oxygen also widens the bronchioles.

ww.No change in diameter: Bronchiole diameter is sensitive to alveolar CO2.

cards.evidence: A greater partial pressure of carbon dioxide in the alveoli causes the bronchioles to increase their diameter as will a decreased level of oxygen in the blood supply, allowing carbon dioxide to be exhaled from the body at a greater rate.

bw: How gases cross the respiratory membrane
cards.tp: Gases follow pressure gradients. The membrane is highly permeable, very thin and has a large surface area.

ww.Active transport: Energy is not required to move oxygen or carbon dioxide across membranes.
ww.Facilitated diffusion: The source describes simple diffusion, with no carrier.

cards.evidence: The actual exchange of gases occurs due to simple diffusion.

bw: Gas exchange with the external environment
cards.tp: It depends on partial pressure differences between the alveoli and the pulmonary capillary blood.

ww.Internal respiration: Internal respiration is gas exchange at the tissues.
ww.Pulmonary ventilation: Ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs.

cards.evidence: External respiration is the exchange of gases with the external environment, and occurs in the alveoli of the lungs.

bw: Gas exchange with the internal environment
cards.tp: Oxygen leaves the blood because tissue PO2 (about 40 mm Hg) is lower than blood PO2 (about 100 mm Hg).

ww.External respiration: External respiration happens in the alveoli.
ww.Cellular respiration: Cellular respiration is the metabolic production of ATP, not gas exchange between blood and tissue.

cards.evidence: Internal respiration is the exchange of gases with the internal environment, and occurs in the tissues.

bw: Pulmonary capillary blood PO2 about 40 mm Hg
cards.tp: This large gradient drives oxygen rapidly across the respiratory membrane into the blood.

ww.About 5 mm Hg: That is the smaller gradient for carbon dioxide.
ww.About 20 mm Hg: The difference between 104 and 40 is about 64.

cards.evidence: This difference is about 64 mm Hg: The partial pressure of oxygen in the alveoli is about 104 mm Hg, whereas its partial pressure in the blood of the capillary is about 40 mm Hg.

bw: Blood returning to the heart from the tissues
cards.tp: Oxygenated hemoglobin makes the blood appear bright red.

ww.Bright red: This is the color of oxygenated blood.
ww.Blue: Deoxygenated blood is burgundy, not blue.

cards.evidence: Hemoglobin that has little oxygen bound to it loses much of its brightness, so that blood returning to the heart is more burgundy in color.

bw: Hemoglobin binds this poison more strongly than oxygen
cards.tp: Increased pressure pushes more oxygen into the blood and displaces carbon monoxide from hemoglobin.

ww.Cyanide poisoning: The source does not link cyanide to hemoglobin binding or hyperbaric treatment.
ww.Pulmonary embolism: An embolism is a blocked pulmonary vessel, not a hemoglobin-binding poison.

cards.evidence: Exposure to and poisoning by carbon monoxide is difficult to reverse, because hemoglobin’s affinity for carbon monoxide is much stronger than its affinity for oxygen, causing carbon monoxide to replace oxygen in the blood.

bw: Killed by high tissue oxygen in a hyperbaric chamber
cards.tp: Anaerobic bacteria cannot or prefer not to live in the presence of oxygen.

ww.Aerobic bacteria: Aerobic bacteria use oxygen, so oxygen is not toxic to them.
ww.Viruses: The source describes oxygen killing anaerobic bacteria.

cards.evidence: An increase in blood and tissue levels of oxygen helps to kill the anaerobic bacteria that are responsible for the infection, as oxygen is toxic to anaerobic bacteria.

bw: Flow of blood in the pulmonary capillaries
cards.tp: Ventilation and perfusion must be matched for efficient gas exchange; gravity effects, blocked ducts or disease can unbalance them.

ww.Ventilation: Ventilation is movement of air into and out of the lungs.
ww.Diffusion: Diffusion is gas movement across the respiratory membrane, not blood flow.

cards.evidence: Ventilation is the movement of air into and out of the lungs, and perfusion is the flow of blood in the pulmonary capillaries.

bw: Perfusion is regulated by blood vessel diameter
cards.tp: Bronchiole diameter responds to alveolar CO2 while pulmonary arteriole diameter responds to alveolar oxygen.

ww.Number of alveoli: The source states ventilation is regulated by airway diameter.
ww.Thickness of the respiratory membrane: Membrane thickness affects diffusion, not the regulation of ventilation.

cards.evidence: Ventilation is regulated by the diameter of the airways, whereas perfusion is regulated by the diameter of the blood vessels.

bw: Total pressure is the sum of partial pressures
cards.tp: Each gas in a mixture exerts its own pressure independent of the others, and gases move from higher to lower partial pressure.

ww.Boyle’s law: Boyle’s law relates the pressure and volume of a gas.
ww.Henry’s law: Henry’s law relates gas concentration in a liquid to solubility and partial pressure.

cards.evidence: Dalton’s law describes the behavior of nonreactive gases in a gaseous mixture and states that a specific gas type in a mixture exerts its own pressure; thus, the total pressure exerted by a mixture of gases is the sum of the partial pressures of the gases in the mixture.

bw: Dissolved gas depends on solubility and pressure
cards.tp: Very little nitrogen dissolves in blood because its solubility is low.

ww.Dalton’s law: Dalton’s law adds partial pressures within a gas mixture.
ww.Boyle’s law: Boyle’s law relates gas pressure and volume.

cards.evidence: Henry’s law states that the concentration of gas in a liquid is directly proportional to the solubility and partial pressure of that gas.

bw: CO2 gradient across the respiratory membrane
cards.tp: Blood about 45 mm Hg versus alveoli about 40 mm Hg. CO2’s much greater solubility compensates for the small gradient.

ww.About 25 mm Hg: The CO2 gradient is far smaller than 25.

cards.evidence: However, the partial pressure difference is less than that of oxygen, about 5 mm Hg.

bw: Share of oxygen carried dissolved in plasma
cards.tp: Oxygen is not very soluble, so most is carried bound to hemoglobin in erythrocytes.

ww.About 25%: Dissolved oxygen is a tiny fraction of the total.
ww.About 50%: Dissolved oxygen is a tiny fraction of the total.

cards.evidence: A small amount of oxygen does dissolve in the blood and is transported in the bloodstream, but it is only about 1.5% of the total amount.

cards.tp: Each hemoglobin molecule has four heme groups, each able to bind one oxygen molecule.

ww.Globin: Globin is the protein portion, which binds carbon dioxide rather than oxygen.
ww.Myoglobin: Myoglobin is a separate muscle protein, not a portion of hemoglobin.

cards.evidence: Heme is the portion of hemoglobin that contains iron, and it is heme that binds oxygen.

bw: Oxygen molecules one hemoglobin can carry at most
cards.tp: Hemoglobin has four subunits, each with an iron-containing heme.

ww.Two: There are four heme groups per hemoglobin.
ww.Eight: There are four heme groups per hemoglobin.

cards.evidence: Each hemoglobin molecule contains four iron-containing heme molecules, and because of this, one hemoglobin molecule is capable of carrying up to four molecules of oxygen.

bw: Normal hemoglobin saturation in a healthy person
cards.tp: Hemoglobin saturation is the percent of heme units bound to oxygen.

ww.60–70 percent: That is far below normal and is seen in extreme altitude.
ww.80–85 percent: Normal saturation is higher than this.

cards.evidence: In a healthy individual with normal hemoglobin levels, hemoglobin saturation generally ranges from 95 percent to 99 percent.

cards.tp: This helps give highly active, heat-producing tissues more oxygen.

ww.They dissociate more slowly: A lower temperature, not a higher one, inhibits dissociation.

cards.evidence: For example, a higher temperature promotes hemoglobin and oxygen to dissociate faster, whereas a lower temperature inhibits dissociation (see Figure 22.26, middle).

cards.tp: Androgens, epinephrine, thyroid hormones and growth hormone stimulate BPG production. Erythrocytes rely on glycolysis because they lack mitochondria.

ww.Carbonic anhydrase: This enzyme converts CO2 and water to carbonic acid.

cards.evidence: BPG promotes the disassociation of oxygen from hemoglobin.

bw: Oxygen-saturated hemoglobin does not readily bind CO2
cards.tp: The Haldane effect helps hemoglobin pick up CO2 at the tissues and release it at the lungs.

ww.Bohr effect: The Bohr effect describes how pH changes hemoglobin’s oxygen affinity.
ww.Chloride shift: The chloride shift is an ion exchange, not a change in hemoglobin affinity.

cards.evidence: The Haldane effect is a phenomenon that arises from the relationship between the partial pressure of oxygen and the affinity of hemoglobin for carbon dioxide.

bw: Main form in which CO2 travels in the blood
cards.tp: Dissolved CO2 is about 7–10 percent and carbaminohemoglobin about 20 percent.

ww.Dissolved CO2: Only 7–10 percent is dissolved in plasma.
ww.Carbaminohemoglobin: About 20 percent travels bound to hemoglobin.

cards.evidence: A large fraction—about 70 percent—of the carbon dioxide molecules that diffuse into the blood is transported to the lungs as bicarbonate.

bw: Converts CO2 and water to carbonic acid
cards.tp: Carbonic acid dissociates into bicarbonate and H+. At the lungs the reaction is reversed by the same enzyme.

ww.Lactate dehydrogenase: This enzyme is not part of CO2 transport in the source.
ww.Hemoglobin: Hemoglobin is a protein carrier, not the enzyme for this reaction.

cards.evidence: Carbonic anhydrase (CA) causes carbon dioxide and water to form carbonic acid (H2CO3), which dissociates into two ions: bicarbonate (HCO3–) and hydrogen (H+).

bw: Bicarbonate leaves erythrocytes in exchange for chloride
cards.tp: Bicarbonate builds up inside erythrocytes and moves down its gradient into the plasma.

ww.Bohr effect: The Bohr effect concerns pH and oxygen release.
ww.Haldane effect: The Haldane effect concerns oxygen and CO2 binding.

cards.evidence: This phenomenon is referred to as the chloride shift and occurs because by exchanging one negative ion for another negative ion, neither the electrical charge of the erythrocytes nor that of the blood is altered.

bw: CO2 bound to globin amino acids
cards.tp: CO2 does not bind iron like oxygen does.

ww.Carboxyhemoglobin: Carboxyhemoglobin is hemoglobin bound to carbon monoxide.

cards.evidence: Carbon dioxide does not bind to iron as oxygen does; instead, carbon dioxide binds amino acid moieties on the globin portions of hemoglobin to form carbaminohemoglobin, which forms when hemoglobin and carbon dioxide bind.

bw: Share of CO2 dissolved in plasma
cards.tp: CO2 is more soluble than oxygen but still needs bicarbonate and hemoglobin for most transport.

ww.30–40 percent: Dissolved CO2 is a smaller fraction than this.
ww.70 percent: That is the fraction carried as bicarbonate.

cards.evidence: Although carbon dioxide is not considered to be highly soluble in blood, a small fraction—about 7 to 10 percent—of the carbon dioxide that diffuses into the blood from the tissues dissolves in plasma.

bw: Acidic pH promotes oxygen release from hemoglobin
cards.tp: More CO2 means more H+ and a lower pH, so oxygen dissociates more readily. Lactic acid also lowers pH.

ww.Haldane effect: The Haldane effect links oxygen levels to hemoglobin’s affinity for CO2.
ww.Chloride shift: The chloride shift is bicarbonate-chloride exchange across the erythrocyte membrane.

cards.evidence: The Bohr effect is a phenomenon that arises from the relationship between pH and oxygen’s affinity for hemoglobin: A lower, more acidic pH promotes oxygen dissociation from hemoglobin.

bw: Ventilation rate unrelated to cellular oxygen needs
Low blood CO2 and high (alkaline) pH
cards.tp: Hyperpnea instead matches ventilation to oxygen demand and does not significantly change blood gases.

ww.Hyperpnea: Hyperpnea meets increased oxygen demand without altering blood gases much.
ww.Eupnea: Eupnea is quiet breathing at rest.

cards.evidence: In contrast, hyperventilation is an increased ventilation rate that is independent of the cellular oxygen needs and leads to abnormally low blood carbon dioxide levels and high (alkaline) blood pH.

bw: Sudden rise in ventilation as exercise begins
Receptors in muscles, joints and tendons
cards.tp: Psychological stimulus and motor neuron activity also drive exercise hyperpnea, since it begins before oxygen falls.

ww.Baroreceptors: Baroreceptors sense pressure in vessels and are not located in muscles and joints.
ww.Aortic body chemoreceptors: Chemoreceptors sense blood gases and pH, which have not yet changed at the start of exercise.

cards.evidence: Finally, physical exertion stimulates proprioceptors, which are receptors located within the muscles, joints, and tendons, which sense movement and stretching; proprioceptors thus create a stimulus that may also trigger the respiratory centers of the brain.

cards.tp: Lower atmospheric pressure makes it harder to reach the same hemoglobin saturation as at sea level.

ww.Percent nitrogen in air: The proportion of nitrogen does not change with altitude either.

cards.evidence: Although the proportion of oxygen relative to gases in the atmosphere remains at 21 percent, its partial pressure decreases (Table 22.4).

cards.tp: This mechanism and a larger fraction of oxygen released to tissues keep tissues supplied at rest at altitude.

ww.Carbonic anhydrase: This enzyme makes carbonic acid from CO2 and water.
ww.Surfactant: Surfactant reduces alveolar surface tension and is made by type II alveolar cells.

cards.evidence: Secondly, at high altitudes, a greater amount of BPG is produced by erythrocytes, which enhances the dissociation of oxygen from hemoglobin.

bw: Caused by low oxygen partial pressure
cards.tp: Serious cases can cause pulmonary or cerebral edema.

ww.Hyperventilation: Hyperventilation is a breathing pattern that lowers blood CO2.
ww.Decompression sickness: This is caused by nitrogen coming out of solution after pressure change, not by altitude hypoxia alone.

cards.evidence: Acute mountain sickness (AMS), or altitude sickness, is a condition that results from acute exposure to high altitudes due to a low partial pressure of oxygen at high altitudes.

bw: Only treatment for acute mountain sickness
cards.tp: Medicines and supplemental oxygen can ease symptoms, but descent is the only treatment.

ww.Ascend faster to acclimate: Slow ascent prevents AMS; going higher makes it worse.

cards.evidence: The only treatment for AMS is descending to a lower altitude; however, pharmacologic treatments and supplemental oxygen can improve symptoms.

cards.tp: This is acclimatization: more red cells carry more oxygen even though each hemoglobin is less saturated.

ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex hormone that retains sodium.
ww.Antidiuretic hormone: ADH is a posterior pituitary hormone that retains water.

cards.evidence: As a result, the kidneys are stimulated to produce the hormone erythropoietin (EPO), which stimulates the production of erythrocytes, resulting in a greater number of circulating erythrocytes in an individual at a high altitude over a long period.

cards.tp: Slow ascent allows the body to acclimate.

ww.Ascend rapidly and exercise hard: Rapid ascent causes AMS and exertion depletes the venous oxygen reserve.

cards.evidence: AMS can be prevented by slowly ascending to the desired altitude, allowing the body to acclimate, as well as maintaining proper hydration.

bw: Volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute
cards.tp: About 20 percent of cardiac output enters the kidneys to be filtered. GFR is about 125 mL/min in men and 105 mL/min in women.

ww.Renal plasma flow: Renal plasma flow is the plasma entering the kidneys, not the filtrate formed.
ww.Net filtration pressure: NFP is a pressure, not a volume per minute.

cards.evidence: The volume of filtrate formed by both kidneys per minute is termed the glomerular filtration rate (GFR).

bw: Average glomerular filtration rate in men
cards.tp: This is about 180 L/day in men and 150 L/day in women, yet only 1–2 L of urine is produced.

ww.About 12.5 mL/min: This is a tenth of the real value.
ww.About 500 mL/min: This is four times the real value.

cards.evidence: On average, this liter results in the production of about 125 mL/min filtrate produced in men (range of 90 to 140 mL/min) and 105 mL/min filtrate produced in women (range of 80 to 125 mL/min).

bw: Created by proteins that stay in the capillary
cards.tp: Bowman’s space has almost no protein, so its osmotic pressure is near zero.

ww.Glomerular blood hydrostatic pressure: This is the force favoring filtration.
ww.Osmotic pressure in Bowman’s space: This is near zero because there are no proteins in the filtrate.

cards.evidence: This means that red and white blood cells, platelets, albumins, and other proteins too large to pass through the filter remain in the capillary, creating an average colloid osmotic pressure of 30 mm Hg within the capillary.

bw: Excess protein leaks into the filtrate
Water moves out of the circulation into tissues
cards.tp: Less osmotic pressure pulls water into the capillaries, so hydrostatic pressure pushes it into the interstitium.

ww.Dehydration: Water is lost from the circulation into tissues rather than from the body.
ww.Hypertension: The described change plumps up tissues; it is not a pressure disorder.

cards.evidence: This “plumps up” the tissues and cells, a condition termed systemic edema.

cards.tp: When pressure drops, the same vessels relax to maintain flow and filtration rate.

ww.It does not respond: Stretching smooth muscle makes it contract, which stabilizes filtration.

cards.evidence: Thus, when blood pressure goes up, smooth muscle in the afferent capillaries contracts to limit any increase in blood flow and filtration rate.

bw: Neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney
cards.tp: Inulin clearance is cumbersome clinically, so creatinine is usually used instead.

ww.Glucose: Glucose is almost fully reabsorbed in the PCT.
ww.Urea: About half of urea is reabsorbed and some is secreted.

cards.evidence: Inulin is a plant polysaccharide that is neither reabsorbed nor secreted by the kidney.

cards.tp: Dosing of drugs excreted by the kidney depends on an accurate GFR estimate.

ww.Inulin: Inulin is a plant polysaccharide given intravenously, not a product of muscle metabolism.
ww.Urea: Urea is partly reabsorbed and comes from protein catabolism in the liver.

cards.evidence: However, since measuring inulin clearance is cumbersome in the clinical setting, most often, the GFR is estimated by measuring naturally occurring creatinine, a protein-derived molecule produced by muscle metabolism that is not reabsorbed and only slightly secreted by the nephron.

cards.tp: The low net pressure means small changes in blood osmolarity or capillary pressure cause large changes in filtrate formed.

ww.About 55 mm Hg: 55 mm Hg is only the glomerular hydrostatic pressure.

bw: MAP needed to keep glomerular filtration going
cards.tp: MAP is the diastolic pressure plus one-third of the pulse pressure. Pressures below this level cause shock.

ww.About 30 mm Hg: Filtration fails well before MAP falls this low.
ww.About 90 mm Hg: A MAP of 90 is a normal value; the threshold is lower.

cards.evidence: Therefore, if you use mean arterial pressure for the GBHP in the formula for calculating NFP, you can determine that as long as mean arterial pressure is above approximately 60 mm Hg, the pressure will be adequate to maintain glomerular filtration.

bw: Water, Na+ and K+ entering the nephron
cards.tp: Almost 100 percent of glucose, amino acids and vitamins are also recovered in the PCT.

ww.About 10 percent: About 10 percent of water reaches the collecting ducts; most is recovered before then.
ww.About 99 percent: 99 percent is the total reabsorbed along the whole nephron.

cards.evidence: About 67 percent of the water, Na+, and K+ entering the nephron is reabsorbed in the PCT and returned to the circulation.

cards.tp: Basal Na+/K+ ATPase keeps Na+ low in the cell; the Na+ gradient then drives glucose in, and glucose leaves by facilitated diffusion.

ww.Simple diffusion: Glucose cannot cross unaided and moves against its gradient.
ww.Primary active transport: The glucose symporter itself uses the Na+ gradient, not ATP directly.

cards.evidence: Glucose reabsorption in the kidneys is by secondary active transport.

cards.tp: The transport maximum for glucose is about 375 mg/min in men and 300 mg/min in women.

ww.Proteinuria: Proteinuria is protein in the urine.
ww.Oliguria: Oliguria is too little urine output.

cards.evidence: Though an exceptionally high sugar intake might cause sugar to appear briefly in the urine, the appearance of glycosuria usually points to type I or II diabetes mellitus.

bw: Water must follow Na+ pumped out of the PCT
cards.tp: Water follows passively to keep the fluid in the peritubular capillary isotonic.

ww.Facultative water reabsorption: Facultative reabsorption is regulated by ADH in the collecting ducts rather than obliged by sodium.
ww.Countercurrent exchange: This describes opposing flows in the vasa recta and loop, not water following sodium.

cards.evidence: This is called obligatory water reabsorption, because water is “obliged” to follow the Na+ (Figure 25.18).

bw: Enzyme in bicarbonate recovery by the PCT
Also used in red blood cells and the stomach
cards.tp: Luminal HCO3- combines with H+ to form carbonic acid, which carbonic anhydrase converts to CO2 and water that enter the cell.

ww.Na+/K+ ATPase: This pump drives the sodium gradient but does not interconvert carbonic acid.
ww.Renin: Renin is the juxtaglomerular enzyme of the RAAS.

cards.evidence: An important enzyme is used to catalyze this mechanism: carbonic anhydrase (CA).

bw: Part of the loop of Henle permeable to water
cards.tp: Up to 15 percent of the water entering the nephron is reabsorbed here.

ww.Thick ascending limb: The ascending limb has no aquaporins and is impermeable to water.
ww.Distal convoluted tubule: The DCT is not part of the loop of Henle.

cards.evidence: These membranes have permanent aquaporin channel proteins that allow unrestricted movement of water from the descending loop into the surrounding interstitium as osmolarity increases from about 300 mOsmol/kg to about 1200 mOsmol/kg.

bw: Loop of Henle section impermeable to water
cards.tp: A Na+/K+/2Cl- symporter moves ions in, driven by the basal Na+/K+ ATPase; this also builds the hyperosmotic medulla.

ww.Descending loop: The descending loop is highly permeable to water.
ww.Collecting duct: Water permeability of the collecting duct depends on ADH.

cards.evidence: As the loop turns to become the ascending loop, there is an absence of aquaporin channels, so water cannot leave the loop.

bw: Loop of Henle and vasa recta
cards.tp: Solute pumps multiply the concentration of Na+ and urea deep in the medulla; the vasa recta must flow slowly to preserve it.

ww.Tubuloglomerular feedback: This is not described in the source as the loop’s concentrating mechanism.
ww.Renin-angiotensin system: The RAAS is a hormonal blood pressure and volume system.

cards.evidence: The structure of the loop of Henle and associated vasa recta create a countercurrent multiplier system (Figure 25.20).

bw: Formed when amino acids are deaminated
cards.tp: Urea is less toxic and helps the loop of Henle and collecting ducts recover water.

ww.Uric acid: The source does not describe uric acid as the deamination product converted to urea.

cards.evidence: Ammonia (NH3) is a toxic byproduct of protein metabolism.

bw: Inserts calcium channels on the luminal surface
cards.tp: Calcitriol also aids calcium recovery by inducing calcium-binding proteins.

ww.Calcitonin: The source does not describe calcitonin acting on the DCT.
ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone regulates Na+ and K+ recovery.

cards.evidence: Receptors for parathyroid hormone (PTH) are found in DCT cells and when bound to PTH, induce the insertion of calcium channels on their luminal surface.

bw: Collecting duct cells with channels for sodium and potassium
Have receptors for ADH and aldosterone
cards.tp: Intercalated cells instead secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate.

ww.Intercalated cells: Intercalated cells handle acid and bicarbonate.
ww.Podocytes: Podocytes are filtration cells of the glomerulus, not collecting duct cells.

cards.evidence: A principal cell possesses channels for the recovery or loss of sodium and potassium.

bw: Secrete or absorb acid or bicarbonate
cards.tp: They play significant roles in regulating blood pH.

ww.Principal cells: Principal cells handle Na+ and K+ and respond to ADH and aldosterone.

cards.evidence: An intercalated cell secretes or absorbs acid or bicarbonate.

bw: Share of filtered water and solutes reabsorbed
cards.tp: Reabsorbed substances return to the circulation by the peritubular capillaries and vasa recta.

ww.About 50 percent: Far more than half is reabsorbed.
ww.About 75 percent: The source says 99 percent of the water is reabsorbed.

cards.evidence: All of these substances were “absorbed” in the digestive tract—99 percent of the water and most of the solutes filtered by the nephron must be reabsorbed.

bw: Raises Na+/K+ ATPase in DCT and collecting duct
cards.tp: Aldosterone also stimulates luminal Na+ and K+ channels in principal cells.

ww.ADH: ADH acts by inserting aquaporins and regulates water, not Na+ pumps.
ww.Parathyroid hormone: PTH induces calcium channels in the DCT.

cards.evidence: Aldosterone increases the amount of Na+/K+ ATPase in the basal membrane of the DCT and collecting duct.

bw: Inserts aquaporins in collecting duct cells
cards.tp: Less ADH means fewer aquaporins, less water recovered and dilute urine.

ww.Angiotensin II: Angiotensin II is a vasoconstrictor that stimulates aldosterone and ADH release.

cards.evidence: When stimulated by ADH, aquaporin channels are inserted into the apical membrane of principal cells, which line the collecting ducts.

bw: Afferent arteriole stretched by rising pressure
cards.tp: When pressure drops, the same smooth muscle relaxes and flow stays even.

ww.Tubuloglomerular feedback: This acts through the macula densa and paracrine signals, not stretch of the arteriole.
ww.Renin-angiotensin mechanism: This is a hormonal mechanism, not an intrinsic stretch response.

cards.evidence: The myogenic mechanism regulating blood flow within the kidney depends upon a characteristic shared by most smooth muscle cells of the body.

bw: Specialized cells in the DCT wall
Sense flow rate and Na+ concentration
cards.tp: Macula densa cells are part of the juxtaglomerular apparatus and drive tubuloglomerular feedback.

ww.Juxtaglomerular cells: JG cells are in the afferent arteriole wall and secrete renin.

cards.evidence: Specialized macula densa cells in this segment of the tubule respond to changes in the fluid flow rate and Na+ concentration.

bw: Paracrine signal that relaxes the afferent arteriole
Fine-tunes the effect of ATP and adenosine
cards.tp: NO relaxes the afferent arteriole at the same time ATP and adenosine make it contract.
cards.evidence: Thus, NO fine-tunes the effects of adenosine and ATP on GFR.

bw: Pressure difference needed for normal GFR
cards.tp: Because the margin is so small, tiny changes in afferent arterial pressure can change GFR significantly.

ww.About 40 mm Hg: The required differential is much smaller.
ww.About 100 mm Hg: The required differential is much smaller.

cards.evidence: Only a 10 mm Hg pressure differential across the glomerulus is required for normal GFR, so very small changes in afferent arterial pressure significantly increase or decrease GFR.

bw: Enzyme made by JG cells of the afferent arteriole
cards.tp: Renin release is stimulated by prostaglandins and NO from the JGA when extracellular fluid volume falls.

ww.Angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE): ACE makes angiotensin II from angiotensin I.
ww.Aldosterone: Aldosterone is an adrenal cortex steroid.

cards.evidence: Renin is an enzyme that is produced by the juxtaglomerular (JG) cells of the afferent arteriole at the JGA.

cards.tp: Its release follows angiotensin II or directly follows raised plasma K+.

ww.Antidiuretic hormone: ADH comes from the posterior pituitary and conserves water.
ww.Atrial natriuretic hormone: ANH promotes sodium loss, the opposite of aldosterone.

cards.evidence: Aldosterone, often called the “salt-retaining hormone,” is released from the adrenal cortex in response to angiotensin II or directly in response to increased plasma K+.

bw: Steroid that binds the aldosterone receptor
Water retention in some phases of the menstrual cycle
cards.tp: It only weakly stimulates Na+ reabsorption and is unimportant in men because circulating levels are low.

ww.Testosterone: The source does not link testosterone to the aldosterone receptor.
ww.Oxytocin: Oxytocin is a peptide hormone and not a steroid.

cards.evidence: It may cause increased retention of water during some periods of the menstrual cycle in women when progesterone levels increase.

bw: Often prescribed to lower blood pressure
cards.tp: Diuretics interfere with the recapture of solutes and water from the forming urine. ADH does the opposite.

ww.Antidiuretics: These, like ADH, promote water recovery.
ww.Vasopressors: These raise blood pressure by vasoconstriction.

cards.evidence: Diuretics are drugs that can increase water loss by interfering with the recapture of solutes and water from the forming urine.

bw: Chronically elevated in diabetic kidney disease
cards.tp: Endothelins also lower GFR by damaging podocytes and constricting both afferent and efferent arterioles.
cards.evidence: On the other hand, in people with diabetic kidney disease, endothelin is chronically elevated, resulting in sodium retention.

bw: Peptides that make the kidneys excrete sodium
cards.tp: They inhibit aldosterone and ADH release, so both Na+ and water recovery fall.

ww.Mineralocorticoids: Mineralocorticoids such as aldosterone retain sodium.

cards.evidence: Natriuretic hormones are peptides that stimulate the kidneys to excrete sodium—an effect opposite that of aldosterone.

bw: Effect on phosphate in the PCT
cards.tp: Losing phosphate in urine prevents calcium phosphate forming in plasma, so circulating calcium can be higher.

ww.Stimulates phosphate reabsorption: PTH causes phosphate to be lost in the urine.
ww.Has no effect on phosphate: The source lists blocking phosphate reabsorption as a PTH action.

cards.evidence: It also blocks reabsorption of phosphate (PO3–), causing its loss in the urine.

bw: Made in the lungs, binds renal arteriole endothelium
cards.tp: ACE converts inactive angiotensin I into active angiotensin II. ACE inhibitors are prescribed for high blood pressure.

ww.Renin: Renin is made by JG cells in the kidney.
ww.Angiotensin II: Angiotensin II is a hormone, the product of ACE.

cards.evidence: ACE is not a hormone but it is functionally important in regulating systemic blood pressure and kidney function.

bw: Helps set the resting membrane potential
cards.tp: Low blood and CSF potassium reflects the sodium-potassium pumps in cell membranes.

ww.Sodium: Sodium is the major extracellular cation.
ww.Calcium: Calcium is mostly bound in bone and is not the main intracellular cation.

cards.evidence: Potassium is the major intracellular cation.

cards.tp: Chloride follows sodium in renal secretion and reabsorption.

ww.Bicarbonate: Bicarbonate is the second most abundant anion in the blood.
ww.Phosphate: Phosphate is a major constituent of the ICF.

cards.evidence: Chloride is the predominant extracellular anion.

bw: Second most abundant anion in the blood
cards.tp: Bicarbonate is the one ion not normally excreted in urine; the kidneys conserve it for buffering.

ww.Chloride: Chloride is the most abundant extracellular anion.
ww.Phosphate: Phosphate is mainly in bone and the ICF.

cards.evidence: Bicarbonate is the second most abundant anion in the blood.

cards.tp: Swollen red cells carry oxygen less efficiently and may be too large to pass through capillaries.

ww.Cells shrink and dehydrate: Diluted ECF draws water into cells, not out.
ww.Cells are unaffected: Water shifts into cells by osmosis, swelling them.

cards.evidence: The excess water causes swelling of the cells; the swelling of red blood cells—decreasing their oxygen-carrying efficiency and making them potentially too large to fit through capillaries—along with the swelling of neurons in the brain can result in brain damage or even death.

bw: Sweat chloride two to five times normal
cards.tp: Sweat analysis is often used in the diagnosis. Hyperchloremia is also seen with dehydration and aspirin intoxication.

ww.Asthma: Asthma is not hereditary chloride-channel disease and does not raise sweat chloride.
ww.Emphysema: Emphysema is not linked to high sweat chloride.

cards.evidence: In people who have cystic fibrosis, chloride levels in sweat are two to five times those of normal levels, and analysis of sweat is often used in the diagnosis of the disease.

bw: The one ion not normally excreted in urine
Conserved by the kidneys for buffering
cards.tp: Sodium, potassium and chloride are routinely analyzed in a spot urine; calcium and phosphate need a 24-hour collection.

ww.Sodium: Sodium is excreted mainly by the kidneys.

cards.evidence: Bicarbonate is the one ion that is not normally excreted in urine; instead, it is conserved by the kidneys for use in the body’s buffering systems.

cards.tp: Deficiency depletes skeletal calcium stores, giving rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults.

ww.Calcitonin: Calcitonin lowers blood calcium; it does not drive intestinal absorption.

cards.evidence: Calcium is absorbed through the intestines under the influence of activated vitamin D.

cards.tp: In children the same deficiency causes rickets, and it can contribute to osteoporosis.

ww.Paget disease: The source does not link Paget disease to vitamin D deficiency.

cards.evidence: A deficiency of vitamin D leads to a decrease in absorbed calcium and, eventually, a depletion of calcium stores from the skeletal system, potentially leading to rickets in children and osteomalacia in adults, contributing to osteoporosis.

bw: May follow removal of the thyroid gland
cards.tp: The four parathyroid nodules are embedded in the thyroid and can be removed with it.

ww.Hyperparathyroidism: Primary hyperparathyroidism gives high blood calcium.
ww.Hypothyroidism: Hypothyroidism is low thyroid hormone and does not by itself explain low calcium here.

cards.evidence: Hypocalcemia, or abnormally low calcium blood levels, is seen in hypoparathyroidism, which may follow the removal of the thyroid gland, because the four nodules of the parathyroid gland are embedded in it.

bw: Released from the thyroid when blood calcium is high
cards.tp: Osteoblasts remove calcium from the blood and incorporate it into bone matrix.

ww.Parathyroid hormone (PTH): PTH is released when blood calcium falls.
ww.Calcitriol: Calcitriol is made in response to PTH and increases calcium absorption.

cards.evidence: Calcitonin is released from the thyroid gland in response to elevated blood levels of calcium.

bw: Activates osteoclasts to break down bone matrix
cards.tp: PTH also converts vitamin D to calcitriol for intestinal calcium absorption, retains kidney calcium and increases phosphate loss.

ww.Calcitonin: Calcitonin is released when blood calcium is high.

cards.evidence: PTH is released from the parathyroid gland in response to a decrease in the concentration of blood calcium.

bw: Sodium the body actually requires per day
cards.tp: A typical Western diet supplies 130 to 160 mmol/day, which appears to contribute to hypertension in some people.

ww.30 to 40 mmol/day: Requirements are far lower than this.
ww.130 to 160 mmol/day: That is the typical Western intake, far above the requirement.

cards.evidence: People eating a typical Western diet, which is very high in NaCl, routinely take in 130 to 160 mmol/day of sodium, but humans require only 1 to 2 mmol/day.

bw: Major cation of the extracellular fluid
Half of the osmotic gradient across cells
cards.tp: Excess dietary sodium appears to be a major factor in hypertension in some people. Excretion is mainly by the kidneys.

ww.Potassium: Potassium is the major intracellular cation and has little effect on osmotic pressure.
ww.Calcium: Calcium is mostly in bone and is not the main extracellular cation.

cards.evidence: Sodium is the major cation of the extracellular fluid.

bw: Excess water dilutes the blood sodium
Sweating, vomiting or diuretics can cause it
cards.tp: Causes also include sweating, vomiting, diarrhea, diuretics, diabetes and acidosis.

ww.Hypernatremia: Hypernatremia is an abnormally high blood sodium.
ww.Hypokalemia: Hypokalemia is a low blood potassium.

cards.evidence: Hyponatremia is a lower-than-normal concentration of sodium, usually associated with excess water accumulation in the body, which dilutes the sodium.

bw: Heart will not relax and may stop within minutes
cards.tp: It can also cause confusion, numbness and weakened respiratory muscles through partial depolarization of cell membranes.

ww.Hypokalemia: Low potassium hyperpolarizes neuron membranes and reduces their responses.
ww.Hypercalcemia: The seizing, non-relaxing heart is the described effect of high potassium.

cards.evidence: Hyperkalemia, an elevated potassium blood level, also can impair the function of skeletal muscles, the nervous system, and the heart.

cards.tp: The kidneys usually conserve phosphate when it is depleted, but this fails during starvation.
cards.evidence: Hypophosphatemia, or abnormally low phosphate blood levels, occurs with heavy use of antacids, during alcohol withdrawal, and during malnourishment.

bw: Cell destruction dumps it into the ECF
cards.tp: Phosphate is a major constituent of the ICF and of nucleic acids, so cell breakdown raises blood levels.

ww.Hyperkalemia: Hyperkalemia is high potassium, though cell destruction raises that too.

cards.evidence: Hyperphosphatemia, or abnormally increased levels of phosphates in the blood, occurs if there is decreased renal function or in cases of acute lymphocytic leukemia.

bw: Share of the blood’s buffering power from proteins
cards.tp: Protein buffers also account for most buffering inside cells.
cards.evidence: Buffering by proteins accounts for two-thirds of the buffering power of the blood and most of the buffering within cells.

bw: Principal protein of red blood cells
Buffers H+ released when CO2 becomes bicarbonate
cards.tp: The process reverses in the pulmonary capillaries, re-forming CO2 to be exhaled.

ww.Albumin: Albumin is a plasma protein, not the principal red cell protein.
ww.Phosphate: Phosphate is a separate buffer pair, not a protein.

cards.evidence: During the conversion of CO2 into bicarbonate, hydrogen ions liberated in the reaction are buffered by hemoglobin, which is reduced by the dissociation of oxygen.

cards.tp: With 20 times more bicarbonate, the system is best at buffering acid, such as lactic acid and ketone bodies.

ww.1:1: The normal ratio is far higher in favor of bicarbonate.

cards.evidence: Bicarbonate ions and carbonic acid are present in the blood in a 20:1 ratio if the blood pH is within the normal range.

bw: Primary buffer of the interstitial fluid around tissue cells
cards.tp: Carbonic acid levels are controlled by the lungs and bicarbonate by the kidneys.

ww.Phosphate buffer: Phosphate is another plasma buffer but not the primary interstitial one.
ww.Hemoglobin buffer: Hemoglobin works inside red blood cells.

cards.evidence: However, the bicarbonate buffer is the primary buffering system of the IF surrounding the cells in tissues throughout the body.

bw: The metabolic part of acid-base balance
cards.tp: The respiratory system controls carbonic acid by exhaling CO2.

ww.The respiratory system: The lungs control carbonic acid through CO2 exhalation.
ww.The digestive system: The source assigns bicarbonate control to the kidneys.

cards.evidence: Whereas the respiratory system (together with breathing centers in the brain) controls the blood levels of carbonic acid by controlling the exhalation of CO2, the renal system controls the blood levels of bicarbonate.

bw: Cells burn fat and make ketone bodies
cards.tp: Ketone bodies are acetoacetic acid, beta-hydroxybutyric acid and acetone, all of which raise blood acidity. A missed insulin dose can start it.

ww.Respiratory alkalosis: Ketone bodies lower pH, whereas respiratory alkalosis comes from losing CO2.
ww.Lactic acidosis: The acid here is ketone bodies from fat breakdown, not lactate.

cards.evidence: Diabetic acidosis, or ketoacidosis, occurs most frequently in people with poorly controlled diabetes mellitus.

cards.tp: Fruity-smelling breath from exhaled acetone is another early sign.

ww.Raise blood bicarbonate: Breathing changes CO2 and carbonic acid, not bicarbonate directly.

cards.evidence: A common early symptom of ketoacidosis is deep, rapid breathing as the body attempts to drive off CO2 and compensate for the acidosis.

bw: Pneumonia or heart failure impair breathing
cards.tp: Hypoventilation from morphine, barbiturates, ethanol or holding the breath can cause it.

ww.Hypocapnia: Hypocapnia is abnormally low blood CO2.
ww.Hypoxemia: Hypoxemia is low arterial oxygen, not high CO2.

cards.evidence: Hypercapnia, or abnormally elevated blood levels of CO2, occurs in any situation that impairs respiratory functions, including pneumonia and congestive heart failure.

cards.tp: It occurs with any cause of hyperventilation that drives off CO2.
cards.evidence: Hypocapnia, or abnormally low blood levels of CO2, occurs with any cause of hyperventilation that drives off the CO2, such as salicylate toxicity, elevated room temperatures, fever, or hysteria.

bw: Fastest way the blood adjusts pH
cards.tp: Buffers act in seconds, the respiratory tract in minutes (by exhaling CO2), the kidneys in hours to days.

ww.Respiratory system: Exhaling CO2 adjusts pH in minutes, not seconds.
ww.Renal system: The kidneys take hours to days.

cards.evidence: It takes only seconds for the chemical buffers in the blood to make adjustments to pH.

cards.tp: The kidneys take hours to days but give the most lasting correction of blood pH.

ww.Respiratory system: Exhaling CO2 adjusts pH within minutes.

cards.evidence: The renal system can also adjust blood pH through the excretion of hydrogen ions (H+) and the conservation of bicarbonate, but this process takes hours to days to have an effect.

cards.tp: Below 7.35 is acidosis and above 7.45 is alkalosis. Continuous pH below 7.0 or above 7.8 is fatal.

ww.6.80 to 7.20: These values are in the acidotic or dangerous range.
ww.7.50 to 7.80: These values are in the alkalotic range.

cards.evidence: Normal arterial blood pH is restricted to a very narrow range of 7.35 to 7.45.

cards.tp: Blood is not truly acidic until pH drops below 7, so this is physiological acidosis.

ww.Hypercapnia: Hypercapnia is high CO2, which can cause acidosis but is not the pH state itself.

cards.evidence: A person who has a blood pH below 7.35 is considered to be in acidosis (actually, “physiological acidosis,” because blood is not truly acidic until its pH drops below 7), and a continuous blood pH below 7.0 can be fatal.

cards.tp: A pH above 7.8 is fatal. Symptoms also include cognitive impairment, nausea and vomiting.
cards.evidence: A person who has a blood pH above 7.45 is considered to be in alkalosis, and a pH above 7.8 is fatal.

cards.tp: The most common cause is organic acids or excessive ketone bodies in the blood.

ww.Respiratory acidosis: Respiratory acidosis is excess CO2 and carbonic acid.
ww.Metabolic alkalosis: Metabolic alkalosis is excess bicarbonate with high pH.

cards.evidence: Metabolic acidosis occurs when the blood is too acidic (pH below 7.35) due to too little bicarbonate, a condition called primary bicarbonate deficiency.

bw: Loss of bicarbonate through the GI tract
cards.tp: Other causes include uremia, ketoacidosis, strenuous exercise, aspirin overdose and certain ingested alcohols.

ww.Vomiting: Vomiting loses stomach acid and tends toward metabolic alkalosis.
ww.Hyperventilation: Hyperventilation blows off CO2 and causes respiratory alkalosis.

cards.evidence: Other causes of metabolic acidosis are a decrease in the excretion of hydrogen ions, which inhibits the conservation of bicarbonate ions, and excessive loss of bicarbonate ions through the gastrointestinal tract due to diarrhea.

bw: Loss of stomach acid by vomiting
cards.tp: Diuretic-induced potassium depletion and laxative overuse can also cause it.

ww.Respiratory alkalosis: Respiratory alkalosis comes from losing CO2 by hyperventilation.

cards.evidence: Metabolic alkalosis is the opposite of metabolic acidosis.

bw: Excess carbonic acid from too much CO2
cards.tp: Bicarbonate is normal at first; if the kidneys compensate, bicarbonate rises.

ww.Metabolic acidosis: Metabolic acidosis is a bicarbonate deficiency rather than CO2 excess.

cards.evidence: Respiratory acidosis occurs when the blood is overly acidic due to an excess of carbonic acid, resulting from too much CO2 in the blood.

bw: Hyperventilation from fear, fever or hypoxia
cards.tp: Catecholamine excess can drive it, and aspirin overdose can also lead to it as the body compensates for initial acidosis.
cards.evidence: Respiratory alkalosis occurs when the blood is overly alkaline due to a deficiency in carbonic acid and CO2 levels in the blood.

cards.tp: This raises blood bicarbonate and reestablishes the proper bicarbonate to carbonic acid ratio.

ww.Excrete bicarbonate and reabsorb H+: That is the renal response to respiratory alkalosis.
ww.Increase exhaled CO2: The primary problem is the lungs, so the kidneys, not breathing, compensate.

cards.evidence: In cases of respiratory acidosis, the kidney increases the conservation of bicarbonate and secretion of H+ through the exchange mechanism discussed earlier.
